scenes.title: Git: Staging, Commits & History
scenes.narration: Git's staging area is what gives you precise control over exactly which changes go into each commit.

scenes.title: The Three Areas
scenes.narration: Your changes begin in the working directory where you edit files. Running git add promotes selected changes into the staging area, a holding zone for the next snapshot. Then git commit records everything staged into the permanent history.

scenes.title: Why Staging Exists
bullets: It lets you commit related changes together while leaving unrelated ones for later.
It gives you a chance to review exactly what will be saved before committing.
It keeps your history clean and each commit focused on a single idea.
scenes.narration: The staging area exists so you can craft deliberate commits rather than dumping everything at once. You can group only the changes that belong together and hold back the rest. This review step keeps each commit focused, which makes the history far easier to read later.

scenes.title: Committing and Reviewing
scenes.code:
git add etl.py            # stage one file
git diff --staged         # review what's staged
git commit -m "Add ETL step"
git log --oneline         # scan the history
git show HEAD             # inspect last commit
scenes.narration: Here we stage a single file so the commit stays focused, then use git diff --staged to review precisely what will be recorded. The commit captures it with a clear message. Afterward git log --oneline gives a compact history, and git show reveals the full detail of any commit.

scenes.text: Write commit messages in the imperative mood — 'Add validation' not 'Added stuff' — and keep each commit to one logical change.
scenes.narration: Good commits are small and single-purpose, with messages phrased as commands like 'Add validation'. This discipline turns your history into clear documentation of how the project grew.
